As of 345 AM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong onshore flow, cooler temperatures, and rainy 
conditions will continue today as cold air damming stays parked
over the area.

Current radar imagery shows widespread heavy drizzle across the CWA, 
with a nearly stationary band of rainfall from west of Farmville to 
Cambridge that has been putting out very efficient rainfall rates in 
spots. Observations are limited, but a gauge in southwestern 
Powhatan has recorded 5.36" in 3-4 hours. The heavier part of 
the band is just to the east of that gauge right along the 
Appomattox River. Radar is estimating around 3.5-5" along the 
border points of Cumberland, Powhatan, and Amelia Counties. The 
Appomattox River from Farmville to Mattoax is starting to show a
response from the rain, so will have to keep an eye on it if 
this band doesn't move soon as the water makes its way 
downstream. Speaking of, the latest hi-res guidance keeps this 
band around well into the morning hours, but potentially 
expanding in coverage to the west and south. Surface analysis 
looks like that it may be positioned along a moisture boundary 
between 925-850mb, sitting along the cold air damming wedge that
has sagged down into our area. There is nothing aloft to move 
these batches of rainfall around as the wedge keeps the 
environment more stagnant, so as we saw yesterday as well, where
rain develops, it could sit for an extended time. Thus, 
localized flash flooding will continue to be a concern through 
the day. Models show coverage may become a bit more scattered 
later this afternoon, with the better rain chances shifting 
southeast/east. 

High temperatures will range from the lower 60s for the northwest 
half of the CWA to low to mid 70s for the SE, with the higher end of 
that range along the immediate coast. It may feel a bit chillier 
outside to some today because in addition to the well-below normal 
temperatures, NE winds will also remain elevated. Inland areas will 
see gusts to 20-25mph. Coastal locations will keep the strongest 
winds as gusts to 30-40mph are likely. The entirety of our Atlantic 
coastline (including Ocean City, Chincoteague, Virginia Beach, and 
Corolla) are expected to have gusts upwards of 45-50mph, not
only for the day today, but persisting through Thursday night -
a Wind Advisory is in effect. This will cause dangerously high 
surf, beach erosion, and multiple rounds of moderate to major 
coastal flooding. See below for more details. 

There may be another round of widespread heavy drizzle during the 
late evening and into the overnight hours as more moisture rotates 
around the low pressure developing offshore. Low temperatures 
will be a few degrees cooler tonight with low to mid 50s 
expected west of I-95. 



KEY MESSAGE 2...Rain chances gradually shift east Thursday, 
potentially making for a dry end to the week. Gusty winds will 
persist. 

Rain chances look to become more confined to eastern portions of the 
area Thursday as the low becomes a bit better organized offshore and 
the persistent ridge of high pressure over southeastern Canada 
begins to break down. This will allow the wedge to weaken over us on 
later Thursday as well. Additional rounds of light rain will likely 
come ashore throughout the day keeping the drizzly skies around for 
everyone through mid-day, then shifting to primarily the eastern CWA 
by the afternoon hours. As mentioned above, NE winds will remain 
strong along the coast again on Thursday (gusts to 35-50mph - 
strongest along the Atlantic) with inland locations seeing breezes 
to 20-25mph. We'll be able to squeeze another well-below normal day 
of high temperatures out of the cold air damming wedge, topping out 
in the low to mid 60s for the west and even lower 70s for the coast. 

The coastal low looks to finally starting moving slowly northward 
Thursday night. Our winds will turn more northerly allowing drier 
air to filter in. Dewpoints may even drop into the upper 40s across 
the west. This will make for our coolest night of the week as 
lows bottom out in the upper 40s across the far west (Louisa, 
Fluvanna, Prince Edward, western Lunenburg), low to mid 50s 
inland, and lower 60s along the coast. Slight model differences 
then impact the forecast for Friday and into the weekend, though
they're closer in agreement than they were 24 hours ago. The 
GFS has the better solution for us, quickly taking the low up 
offshore of Massachusetts by Friday night and keeping it up 
there through the weekend. The ECMWF lingers the low offshore of
our area through Saturday, then finally lifts it north. The NBM
guidance falls more in line with the GFS, so have kept 
lingering rain chances along the immediate coastline through the
day on Friday. West of I-95 should start to see some clearing 
skies. Highs on Friday will begin to warm back up while still
